bio.en: Melissa Tan was the longtime head of growth for Dropbox's B2B business and its first growth PM, later advising companies like Canva, Grammarly, and Miro on growth.
bio.zh: 梅丽莎·谭（Melissa Tan）曾是 Dropbox B2B 业务长期的增长负责人及第一位增长 PM，后来为 Canva、Grammarly、Miro 等公司提供增长咨询。

summary.en: Melissa shares how hiring smart people with no sales background at Dropbox led to unexpectedly innovative go-to-market motions. She champions first-principles thinking over copying playbooks. The episode offers grounded growth advice drawn from scaling one of the most iconic B2B products.
summary.zh: 梅丽莎分享了在 Dropbox 雇佣毫无销售背景的聪明人，反而催生出意料之外的创新获客打法。她推崇"第一性原理思考"，而非照搬套路。本期提供了来自打造最具标志性 B2B 产品之一的扎实增长建议。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: My aha moment of the value of first principles thinking was when I was at Dropbox. We would hire a ton of really smart people that had never done sales and had them do sales. There are a lot of disadvantages to that, but I do think it led to a ton of innovation. That's how we got our very innovative go-to market motions because a lot of those people then moved into different functions at the company. They had all this context on who the user was. They had talked to so many different users at that point. If you take people that are just super smart, they've never done it before, one advantage of that is they can innovate because I think they come in with, I don't know anything. Let me just figure this out.
turns.zh: 我在 Dropbox 时突然意识到第一性原理思维的价值所在。我们当时招了大量从未从事过销售工作的极其聪明的人，让他们去负责销售业务。这种做法固然有诸多弊端，但我认为它确实催生了大量创新成果。比如，我们推出了极具创新性的市场推广策略，原因就在于许多这些员工后来转入了公司的其他部门。他们对用户群体有了深刻的理解，因为他们此前已与大量不同类型的用户进行了深入沟通。若招来那些天赋异禀却毫无销售经验的人才，其一个优势在于他们能激发创新思维——因为他们往往会带着"我一无所知"的谦逊态度，积极探索未知领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So before we get into it too deeply, I want to first talk about Dropbox. So you're at Dropbox for four-ish years, something like that, doing a lot of their growth work and it was in the middle of a lot of their growth spurts and things like that. And when I think Dropbox and growth, there's kind of this dichotomy I think about. On the one hand, there's just these incredible growth loops that work, this referral program, this crazy word of mouth. There's just this explosive growth story of a product. (00:07:11): And then on the other hand, there's this B2B side that from an outsider just feels like that's something that didn't work for a long time. And then Box came around and did that really well, and I think Dropbox has done better since then, but it feels like this combination of really successful growth and then maybe less successful. So I'm curious, just looking back from your experience and from what you've heard, what do you think Dropbox did and what do you think they did wrong? And then just what are some learnings from that experience and watching Dropbox go through that?
turns.zh: 在我们深入探讨之前，我想先聊聊Dropbox。你在Dropbox工作了大约四年，主要负责推动其业务增长，当时正值公司高速发展的阶段。每当想到Dropbox和增长，我总会联想到一种矛盾心理。一方面，Dropbox凭借推荐计划、口口相传等手段实现了爆炸式增长，堪称产品成功的典范。（00:07:11）但另一方面，作为外行人看来，他们的B2B业务板块长期未能取得理想效果。后来Box成功扭转了局面，而Dropbox也取得了显著进步。不过这种成功与挫折交织的局面，让人不禁好奇——从你的亲身经历和所闻所知来看，你认为Dropbox做对了什么？又犯了哪些错误？从这段历程中能汲取哪些宝贵经验？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. And having been at Dropbox for close to five years, I did a lot of reflection while I was there. So I was there from 2013 to 2017, around 200 people. I think about a billion dollar valuation to essentially ... I think when I left we were 1,500 people and we're valued at 10 billion at the IPO. I think the things that Dropbox got right, one of them was definitely hiring. So when I think about 2013, Dropbox was actually known in the tech circles as a place that was very selective, very difficult to get into. You could have an amazing resume, and Dropbox was really selective about the type of people they brought in. So I think they looked for two main things. They looked for first principles thinkers, so not necessarily your experience, but how do you approach problems, how do you know the right questions to ask? And then create your own framework around that. (00:08:32): Dropbox also hired for people that were just really humble, collaborative and team oriented. And the combination of those two things, people that were just first principle thinkers also just really collaborative to tons of innovation. And so when you think about freemium product led growth, even we created a high velocity sales motion there, there was just so much innovation because you had these folks that just knew how to solve problems and worked really well cross-functionally across product growth, sales, et cetera. (00:09:04): And also, broadly speaking, the company just infused the topic of hiring and recruiting into the culture. It was something that as I was there, everyone knew we were all going to be spending a ton of time interviewing. We all were trained on how to sell Dropbox and how to sell the roles we were recruiting for too so that we could close top talent. So I think that's something we definitely got and I learned a ton about. The other thing was the importance of execution. (00:09:28): So a lot of times at Dropbox we would try something and it didn't work the first time around and it was easy to be maybe say that just doesn't work for us, like growth. We actually had tried to do some growth experiments back in 2013 and they didn't find much traction, but what we found is the devil, I like to say the devils and the details and the devils and how you execute. And so coming back to how do we execute just a little bit differently and some of the learnings there where I think the first time we started growth, we could have been more user-centric and been a lot more hypothesis driven. We were following a lot of best practices that just didn't really apply to Dropbox. (00:10:04): And so the way that you execute ends up really mattering. That was the second learning. The third is just focus. I think you alluded to this, I think the blessing and the curse of early success is that you can get pulled in so many different directions and Dropbox had a consumer business, a B2B business, and I think we could have clarified what is our point of view on what the overall motion should look like, how do we blend and think about the journey from consumer to B2B really early on, and I think a learning was that we just started our sales motion and our enterprise a little bit later than we should have and a lot of competition caught up to us. (00:10:44): And then finally, I think the fourth one that I really believe in is how do you engage the whole company in thinking about go-to-market growth and revenue. Back in 2013, in tech growth was kind of like this dirty word and revenue was a dirty word, and so we were like, "Oh, a good product should sell itself. And it wasn't until our self-serve business started to slow down that we started our team because we realized there's a ton of opportunity in just optimizing the experience. (00:11:10): And because we started a bit later, it always felt like growth was a layer on top of product. I think the best way to execute is just to have that be front and center from the start. What is our go-to market strategy? How are we thinking about monetization and having that infused into how you think about product development? And that's something both JZ who leads product at Webflow and myself been really intentional as we've thought of the collaboration across product and growth. So that was definitely a learning. So I guess the four things there are just the importance of hiring, execution. Think about your go-to market early on and then how do you engage the whole company on thinking about go-to market and growth.
turns.zh:
是的，这确实是个很棒的问题。在Dropbox工作了近五年期间，我做了很多反思。2013年至2017年间，我在那里共待了约200人，当时估值约10亿美元，而我离开时公司已有1500人，IPO时估值达100亿美元。我认为Dropbox做对的几件事之一，就是招聘策略。2013年，Dropbox在科技圈被誉为一家选拔严格、极难加入的公司。即便你简历出色，他们对人才的筛选也极为严格。他们主要看重两点：一是首要原则思维者——不看重经验，而是看你如何解决问题、如何提出正确的问题，并围绕这些问题建立自己的框架。（00:08:32）Dropbox还招聘那些谦逊、善于合作、以团队为导向的人。两者的结合——既有首要原则思维者，又具备团队协作能力——催生了大量创新。即使是免费增值的产品主导型增长策略，我们也成功建立了高效的销售团队，因为团队成员善于跨职能协作，涵盖产品、增长、销售等多个领域。（00:09:04）此外，公司将招聘文化深深融入企业基因。在那里，每个人都知道自己需要花大量时间面试候选人。我们接受过如何推销Dropbox以及招聘岗位的专业培训，这样才能吸引顶尖人才。另一个关键点是执行力的重要性。（00:09:28）Dropbox曾多次尝试新策略但未获成功，比如2013年的增长实验未能取得预期效果。但我们发现，真正的问题在于细节、执行细节和团队协作方式。例如，早期增长策略本可以更以用户为中心、更基于假设验证，但当时我们盲目遵循通用最佳实践，导致策略偏离实际。（00:10:04）最后，专注力至关重要。我认为你们已经提到过这一点——早期成功既是福也是祸。Dropbox同时运营消费级业务和B2B业务，但我们未能早期明确整体增长战略方向，未能及早规划从消费级到B2B的转型路径，最终被竞争对手超越。（00:10:44）最后，第四条经验是如何让全公司参与到市场增长和营收战略中来。2013年，增长和营收在科技界被视为禁忌词汇。我们当时的观念是，“好产品自然会带来增长”。但后来我们意识到，必须让整个公司树立增长思维，建立从产品到营收的闭环策略。
产品本身就应该具备吸引力。直到我们的自助服务业务开始放缓，我们才组建了增长团队，因为我们意识到，单纯优化用户体验蕴藏着巨大的机遇。（00:11:10）由于我们起步较晚，总觉得增长只是产品开发的附加层。我认为最有效的执行方式，就是从一开始就将增长置于核心位置。我们的市场拓展策略是什么？如何将变现逻辑融入产品开发思维？这正是Webflow产品负责人JZ和我在规划产品与增长协同时始终刻意关注的重点。这确实是一次深刻的启发。所以我认为关键的四点在于：招聘的重视度、执行力的保证、尽早规划市场策略，以及如何让整个公司都参与到市场拓展和增长思维中来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said Dropbox essentially there was a late investment in sales and there's a sense maybe product led growth's going to take us really far. And I imagine look at Jira and Atlassian, they're just all product led and that's amazing. I guess what's your current framework for when it makes sense to start leaning into sales and hiring a sales team for say a product led product that is working?
turns.zh: 你说 Dropbox 基本上是在销售方面投入较晚，可能认为产品主导型增长会带我们走得很远。我想看看 Jira 和 Atlassian，他们完全以产品为主导，这真是了不起。我想问问你，当前对于像产品主导型产品这样正在运作的产品，何时开始倾向于销售并组建销售团队才算合理？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: It really comes down to the product because initially I think most companies are leaning heavier into sales or heavier into product-led. You're usually not doing both at the same time. And so a trend I've seen is starting product-led first and the signal is that is a good motion for you is if the product is really intuitive to onboard onto. There's a low learning curve so you don't need a human to onboard the user. Also, if there's a viral component to it, that is really what can take. (00:12:43): Dropbox is massively viral. When I think also about Miro or Figma, those also are very viral products. Those have a kind of the DNA of product led. And initially I think when you have scale, you're getting a lot of signal on what is resonating with the user. Initially, you also don't have ... It takes a while to build out the features for enterprise. And so as you're building out the product-led motion, you have probably larger companies in your self-serve base and they are often knocking on your door. (00:13:15): This happened at Dropbox being like, "I need you to build SSO for me. I need you to build all these enterprise grade features. It's not secure enough." And so you are also collecting the list of things you need to build on the enterprise side. And so I think it's typically looking like you might start product-led, then go enterprise. And then the other direction I've seen is some companies initially are just more conducive to an enterprise in sales motion. Potentially, you need to build custom things for these users. It's also not a bottom-up motion. Maybe the way you sell the product starts with the legal team or the finance team or some important stakeholder, but then a lot of companies now are trying to make that shift to make the product more accessible and go product led. (00:13:56): And so then you're thinking about, okay, how do I make this product simpler to onboard onto? How do I think about reaching the end user at scale? And so I think it's basically first figuring out where do you start and then starting to invest in the area. And I guess maybe lastly, knowing how the whole picture fits together. There's a lot of companies that do consumer and B2B and I think the earlier you can figure out how they go together and what the paths and journeys look like, it just ends up being more seamless to the user and, yeah.
turns.zh: 这实际上取决于产品本身。我认为大多数公司最初要么更侧重于销售，要么更侧重于产品主导型增长。通常两者不会同时进行。我观察到的一个趋势是，先从产品主导型入手，如果产品对用户上手非常直观，低学习曲线且无需人工引导，那么这就是一个很好的方向。另外，如果产品有病毒式传播的特性，那就更有优势了。（00:12:43）：Dropbox 就是极具病毒性的。想想 Miro 或 Figma 这些产品，它们也是病毒式传播的产品，骨子里就带有产品主导型基因。当你达到一定规模后，就能更清楚哪些功能能真正打动用户。最初，你可能没有……企业级功能的开发需要时间。因此，在推进产品主导型策略时，你的自助服务用户群可能已经相当庞大，他们会主动找上门来。（00:13:15）：Dropbox 就曾遇到过这种情况，比如“我需要你们开发单点登录功能，我需要你们开发所有这些企业级功能，现有安全性不足。”于是你会逐步收集企业级功能的需求清单。因此，我认为通常的路径是先从产品主导型起步，再转向企业级服务。而我见过的另一种情况是，有些公司最初更倾向于企业级销售策略。可能需要为这些用户定制解决方案，这也不是自下而上的过程。销售策略可能从法律团队或财务团队等关键利益相关者开始，但现在很多公司正试图让产品更易用，转向产品主导型。（00:13:56）：然后你会思考，如何让产品更易上手？如何大规模触达终端用户？所以关键是先确定起点，然后在该领域投入资源。最后，我想知道整个拼图如何拼合起来。很多公司同时做消费级和 B2B 业务，我认为越早理清两者的关联，规划出清晰的路径和用户旅程，最终对用户来说就越无缝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so let me start to transition into talking about building awesome teams and high performing teams. And something that I know about you that I've heard from other people is that you have this reputation for being a person that people follow from company to company, which is the ultimate sign of, I don't know, retention and NPS and product market fit as a leader and a manager. So I'm just curious, what is it that you think you do that gets people to follow you from company to company?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来我要转向如何打造优秀团队和高绩效团队。我从别人那里了解到，你有这样一个声誉：能让人们跟着你从一家公司跳到另一家公司。这是作为领导者和管理者在留存率、净推荐值和产品市场契合度方面的最高荣誉。所以我很好奇，你认为自己做了哪些能让人们追随你的事情？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I've been really fortunate. I've worked with a few folks from my early Dropbox team that I've known for 10 years now, like a couple of times. In some case, three times. And I always feel so privileged that I get the opportunity to work with them again and they have that trust and confidence in me. I think what it is, and it took me time to develop this, is I have a very people focused approach to how I lead and manage. I really think the core of it is deeply caring about people, building that trust, investing in their career development, helping them figure out where they want to go in their career. I think for me it's very personal. I have been really fortunate to have great mentors and managers that helped me in those respects. And so it really started from just paying it forward and wanting to do the same thing for other people that were on my team. I think it just comes down to deeply caring and everything, all your actions follow through from there. So that's how I would describe that.
turns.zh: 我真的很幸运。我曾与几位早期Dropbox团队的成员共事，他们至今已相识十年，有时甚至三次合作。每次重聚，我都深感荣幸，能有机会再次与他们共事，而他们对我也始终充满信任与信心。我认为这源于我领导和管理时以人为本的理念。我深信其核心在于真心关怀员工，建立信任，投资于他们的职业发展，并帮助他们明确职业方向。对我而言，这份关怀非常个人化。幸运的是，我曾遇到过出色的导师和管理者，他们在这些方面给予我诸多帮助。因此，我最初只是希望将这份善意传递下去，为团队中的每位成员做同样的事。归根结底，就是要真心关怀他人，而你所有的行动都应由此出发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Some people may be hearing that and feel like there's this choice you have to make as a leader deeply care about the person or drive impact, focus on getting the work done. Do you find that those can coexist or is it this kind of two ends of a spectrum and maybe the question's just like how do you do both? How do you help people yes, achieve and drive impact while also feeling like you really care about them?
turns.zh: 有些人听了这些话，可能会觉得作为领导者必须做出选择：要么深切关怀员工，要么专注于推动业务成果、完成工作。你认为这两者能否共存？或者说它们是两个极端，问题在于如何兼顾两者？如何既帮助员工取得成功，又能展现对他们的关怀？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I don't think that they're mutually exclusive of each other because I think the other thing that I really emphasize on my team is being very results oriented. So as a growth leader, for better or for worse, everything you do is very measurable. And so I actually think this is why a lot of folks on my team, something that they actually appreciate is knowing what success looks like and knowing how they'll be measured. And I actually create a very results-oriented culture on the team where it's clear what our goals are, we break it down into the individual levers, it's clear how success is measured for each individual. (00:16:54): And so I don't think they are mutually exclusive. And then my role as a leader is also supporting their career growth, helping them meet those goals and giving them feedback along the way. So even though they might sound like two different things, I actually think they can coexist and for me, I actually really lean into both.
turns.zh: 我认为这两者并非相互排斥。因为我特别强调的团队文化是以结果为导向。作为增长型领导者，无论好坏，你所做的一切都需要量化成效。因此，我认为正因如此，团队中许多成员非常欣赏这样的理念——他们清楚成功的标准，也明白如何被衡量。我在团队中营造了以结果为导向的文化：目标明确，分解到每个层面，个人绩效评估清晰。（00:16:54）所以我认为两者并非不可兼得。作为领导者，我的职责还包括支持他们的职业发展，帮助他们达成目标，并在过程中给予反馈。因此，尽管这两者听起来像是两个不同维度，但我认为它们可以共存，而我个人也确实在两者之间找到平衡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of caring deeply about someone and being that kind of leader? People may be listening and are like, "Oh yeah, I care a lot about my reports." But what are some examples of what that means to you that maybe would surprise people?
turns.zh: 能举个深切关怀他人的例子吗？人们可能会说：“哦，是的，我很关心我的下属。”但你对此的理解能让人们感到惊讶吗？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I think an example from someone that they joined my team and I just early on thought that they weren't maybe moving quickly enough and they needed some more direction. And so really early into them joining the company, that was about two or three weeks in, I actually pulled them aside and I said, "Hey, we need to move a lot faster. This is where we need to get to by X. We're a growth team. We need to prove wins out early. This is how I think we should do it. Let's try to create a roadmap, a list of problems to solve, et cetera, hypotheses." And they don't have to be right, but just getting something out there, starting to line the whole team on what those are and then defining how we're going to measure success and know we're in the right path. We just need to get there as quickly as we can. (00:18:14): And so I gave them that feedback and afterwards, ever since then they have been just on a tear and they actually have mentioned that in later conversations a year into working together that they were so grateful that I had that conversation with them and that I took the time to tell them those things. I think sometimes as a manager it can maybe, you want to avoid the uncomfortable conversations, but I actually think the more direct you can be but also saying this is my intention. My intention is to set you up for success. That goes really far and I think that's a great example of how do you deeply care about somebody and give them direct feedback and you're giving them direct feedback because you deeply care and you also believe that they can do things differently. I think the only reason you would give that feedback is because they can do things differently and you just want to help support them.
turns.zh: 我想举个例子，当时有人加入我的团队，我一开始就觉得他们进展不够快，需要更多的指导。所以在他们加入公司的头两三周，我就私下跟他们聊了聊，说：“嘿，我们需要加快进度。这是我们要达成的目标。我们是增长团队，需要尽早证明成果。我觉得我们应该这么做。先制定路线图，列出待解决的问题，提出假设。”这些想法不一定正确，但关键是先把思路提出来，在整个团队中达成共识，然后明确衡量成功的标准，确保我们走在正确的道路上。我们只需要尽快达成目标。（00:18:14）后来我给他们反馈后，从那以后他们就像开挂了一样。一年后的后续交流中，他们提到非常感激我当时的对话，也感激我花时间给他们这些建议。我认为作为管理者，可能有时会想避免那些令人不适的对话，但我觉得越直接越好，只要表明这是出于善意。我觉得这就是一个很好的例子，如何深切关心某个人，给予他们直接反馈，而这种关怀源于你相信他们能有所不同。唯一的出发点就是希望他们能有所改进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In that conversation. What is it that you did that made them feel like you really cared about them? Because when I hear you describe it's like you're just telling them, you're giving them feedback just like, "Hey, you need to do a lot better at this. We need to actually hit our goals." What was it that made them feel like, "Oh, she really wants me to succeed?"
turns.zh: 在那次对话中，你做了什么让他们觉得你真的很关心他们？因为听你描述，你只是告诉他们，‘嘿，你在这方面需要做得更好，我们需要达成目标。’是什么让他们觉得‘哦，她真的希望我成功？’

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I think in that conversation what's important is also saying, "I believe you can do all these things and I'm doing this to support you." Or, "I'm sharing this feedback because I believe in you." Also saying that I'm here as support, as you are building that out, let me know what I can do to support you. We can jam on it together if it's helpful. Basically, I guess boil it down to one, restating your intention and why you are having that conversation to sharing that you are there to support them and offering your own help as well. (00:19:59): Those I think are the things that go along well. And I think the third thing is as you give someone feedback, it should never sound like finger pointing or criticizing. It's really just, "Hey, this is what I observed, this is the impact that it had and here is a different way." And so keeping the feedback really about the work itself and the specific things that you think can be improved.
turns.zh: 我认为在那次对话中，重要的是要说，‘我相信你能做到这些，我这样做是为了支持你’，或者‘我分享这些反馈是因为我相信你’。还要说，我会在你推进过程中提供支持，如果有帮助的话，让我知道怎么做。基本上，我觉得可以归结为三点：重申你的意图和对话的目的，表明你会支持他们，并主动提供帮助。（00:19:59）我认为这些做法很有效。第三点是，当你给别人反馈时，绝不能听起来像是在指责或批评。只是说，‘嘿，这是我观察到的，这带来了什么影响，这里有不同的做法。’所以反馈要始终围绕工作本身，以及你认为可以改进的具体方面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you're also a big fan of developing talent internally versus hiring experts from the outside and it's always this decision I think as a leader and as a company. How much do you invest in developing people knowing they can leave anytime, knowing that that's going to take all this time and work? What have you found from and just learned about the advantages maybe of spending time in developing people and helping them progress and just why is that something you find really important?
turns.zh: 我知道你也非常赞同在公司内部培养人才，而非从外部聘请专家。我认为，作为领导者和企业主，始终面临着这样的抉择。当知道员工随时可能离职，知道这需要耗费大量时间和精力去培养人才时，你又会投入多少资源？从你自身经历来看，你发现了哪些优势，或是学到了哪些经验？为何你认为在人才培养上投入如此重要？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I'll start with the why behind developing people. For me personally, it comes from like I'm personally passionate about it just because I feel that a lot of folks invested in me personally when I started out in the working world, I actually struggled quite a lot. I think making the transition from school where it's really clear what success looks like, you're just studying, getting good grades. To work where things are much more ambiguous was a really big transition for me and I really benefited from so many mentors that invested in me that I kept in touch with over the years that have also just helped me with my careers. (00:21:30): Two that really stand out are from Dropbox, Oliver Jay who goes by OJ and GC Lionetti. So it really has come from a very personal place for me. Secondly, I think it's just makes a lot of sense as you're scaling a company that as you are growing, it just is a smoother transition that the folks on your team can grow with you. People will build institutional knowledge and people talk a lot about founder intuition and that intuition that founders just have. I actually think that extends to early employees too, that have built a ton of context on the user on how to get things done at the company. So the more that you develop talent within the company, the smoother transition is versus bringing someone from the outside where there's just a lot of different factors and there's risk there. And so it really comes from a personal place, but also it makes a lot of sense from just like de-risking the situation as you're scaling.
turns.zh: 首先，我来说说为什么要培养人才。对我个人而言，源于对这项工作的热情。因为当我刚踏入职场时，曾有很多人帮助过我，而那时的我确实遇到了很多挑战。我认为，从校园生活到职场的转变非常困难——校园里成功的标准清晰明确，而职场中却充满不确定性。这段过渡对我来说很艰难，多年来与我保持联系、帮助我职业发展的导师们，对我意义非凡。（00:21:30）其中最令我难忘的是Dropbox的Oliver Jay（人称OJ）和GC Lionetti。培养人才源于我个人的经历。其次，从公司扩张的角度来看，当团队成员能与公司共同成长时，过渡会更加顺畅。人们会积累机构知识，也常谈及创始人的直觉——这种直觉不仅适用于创始人，早期员工也积累了大量公司运营的上下文知识。因此，内部培养人才比从外部引进更能降低扩张风险。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In my personal career I had the biggest inflection point and the most progress I made as a product manager was one manager who just did exactly what you're describing, where you invested really deeply in helping me become a better PM and it was not easy. It was just very critical of all the things I wasn't doing perfectly. And I always think about people don't sometimes have someone like that in their career. They don't have a manager like Melissa. Do you have any advice for people that are looking for someone like that or they're just like, "Man, I have no one around me that's really helping me develop?" What do you suggest they do?
turns.zh: 在我个人职业生涯中，担任产品经理期间最大的转折和成长来自一位经理，他完全践行了你所描述的培养模式。他深度投入，帮助我成为更优秀的产品经理，这绝非易事。他会严厉指出我做得不够好的地方。我总在想，很多人职业生涯中都缺少这样的导师。例如，他们没有梅利莎这样的经理。对于那些正在寻找这类导师的人，或者正感叹“天啊，我身边没有真正帮助我成长的人”的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: As you are looking for a job, I actually do think you should look to work with people that have that reputation and that you can see that interest that they enjoy mentoring people. They have a track record of developing people. Maybe they have brought other people they've worked with at the company from other companies. Those are good signals that that's something that that person cares about. And even in the interview process, kind of interviewing your manager too and understanding what is their management philosophy, how do they think about your career path in that role? Those are things I would look for. (00:23:32): The second thing too is as you're interviewing, looking for a manager who especially your success will be tied to their success, this is actually what happened. I mean it's not like you need to be super strategic about that, but when I reflect back at times when I got closest to people was when I was one of the most critical people on their team and they really needed me to be successful and so they also just would spend a ton more time with me. (00:23:58): So really looking for those opportunities and being really selective in the types of roles you're taking. I also think there have been times for me personally where I've built relationships with someone that wasn't my direct manager that worked at the same company. And this actually has happened a lot at other companies I've worked with where someone knows that it's a passion of mine to mentor people. And so they proactively reach out to me, ask me for advice, ask me, "Hey, can we set up a monthly recurring sync?" (00:24:25): And so I also think you can look for other people at the company that you work with. And then finally the other thing is looking for external advisors. I actually, in my advising end up mentoring a lot of the people that I work with too. It just organically ends up happening. And so I would say summarize that as just look for the people that you think have this passion, build that relationship with them. And ideally I think you actually build the strongest when you are working together. You just learn so much about each other, but if you don't have that set up, I think there's other ways to just proactively look for mentorship and guidance.
turns.zh:
既然你正在找工作，我确实认为你应该优先选择那些声誉良好、且能明显看出乐于指导他人的上司。他们在培养人才方面有着出色的业绩记录。或许他们曾将其他公司的人才引入现任公司。这些都是表明对方重视人才培养的信号。甚至在面试过程中，主动了解直属经理的管理理念，以及他们如何看待你在这个岗位上的职业发展路径，这些都是值得关注的细节。（00:23:32）  
第二点是，在面试过程中要寻找那种你的成功与他们的成功息息相关的上司。这并非刻意设计的策略，但回想起来，我与他人关系最融洽的时刻，往往是我在团队中发挥着至关重要的作用，他们迫切希望我能取得成功，因此会为我投入更多精力。（00:23:58）  
因此，要善于把握这些机遇，并在选择职位时保持谨慎。我个人曾与同公司但非直属上司的人建立深厚关系。在其他公司，这种情况也屡见不鲜——有人知道我热衷于指导他人，就会主动联系我，寻求建议，甚至主动提议：“嘿，我们能否每月定期沟通？” （00:24:25）  
最后，可以关注公司内其他同事。总之，要寻找那些拥有相同热情的人，并与他们建立深厚关系。理想情况下，在共同工作中能收获最丰硕的成长成果。但若暂无此条件，也可主动寻求指导与支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any tips on the questions? Maybe to ask a manager to help them get to this, if any come to mind and also when you're looking for someone to help you, anything specific you think that people should look for that maybe they may not be thinking about?
turns.zh: 关于这些问题有什么建议吗？或许可以请直属经理帮助达成目标，或者当你寻找导师时，需要特别关注哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: On the questions to ask when you're interviewing for a role, I would actually ask things like I'd love to get a sense for how you think about ... I mean I think you can flat out ask, I'd like to get a sense of how you think about managing folks on your team, how you think about developing talent on your team and seeing what their responses to that. I would also ask how are you thinking about the career path for this role? And if the person has not thought about it at all or doesn't ask you, "Well, what is important to you?" I think those are some signals that it's maybe not where this person tends to spend their time thinking. And then I would also ask other people on the panel that are not going to be your manager but that work with this person, especially if you happen to talk to people that they manage, how is this person as a manager? And that ends up being also very insightful. (00:26:08): The questions I would ask if you're looking for someone external, I always find that that relationship is best the more organic it could be. I think Cheryl Sandberg had wrote this in her book Lean She basically writes about how some people will go, "Will you be my mentor?" And I've got that question too, and it's just a lot of pressure to get asked that question really early in and you don't really know the person. And so the more it can be organic where you talk to somebody, you have actual advice that you want, some people will just reach out to me that I haven't worked with in a long time and like, "Hey, I'm thinking about a career decision or I'm in this tricky situation at work, can we talk?" And I just give them advice and they will reach out to me for advice occasionally. (00:26:57): It doesn't have to be a recurring thing that you have to just nurture that relationship. I think that is a way to do it. Or if you are working with somebody and you want to set up some type of monthly thing, I think you asked for that as well. The only thing is I would just be respectful of the time. So if you don't have anything to talk about that month or anything like that, I'm just always willing to help people. It doesn't mean we have to be frequently in touch. And so I think it's also less about being frequently in touch and it's just going and reaching out when you actually have a problem. People that want to help others are just going to, if they have the time, they'll say yes.
turns.zh:
关于面试时该问的问题，我实际上会问一些诸如：我希望了解你如何看待……我的意思是，你可以直接问：“我希望了解你如何管理团队中的成员，如何培养团队人才，以及他们的反应如何。” 我还会问：“你对这个职位的职业发展路径有何看法？” 如果对方根本没有思考过这个问题，或者没有主动问你：“那对你来说重要的是什么？”，我认为这些都可能是对方不常深思熟虑的信号。然后我还会询问面试小组中的其他成员，他们虽然不是你的直属上司，但与这个人共事过，特别是如果你恰好和他们管理的下属聊过天，他们会怎么评价这个人作为管理者的表现。这往往也很有启发性。

（00:26:08）：如果是在寻找外部候选人时，我会问的几个问题是，我发现这种关系越自然越好。谢丽尔·桑德伯格在《精益》一书中提到，有些人会问：“你能做我的导师吗？”我也遇到过这种问题，过早被问到这个问题会带来很大压力，因为你对这个人其实并不了解。所以更自然的交流方式更重要。比如，有很久没合作过的人会主动联系我，说：“嘿，我正在考虑职业决策，或者我遇到了工作中的难题，能聊聊吗？”我就会给他们建议，他们偶尔也会向我寻求帮助。

（00:26:57）：这不必是需要刻意维系的关系。我认为这是一种有效的方式。或者如果你正在与某人合作，想要建立某种月度沟通机制，我觉得你也提到了这一点。唯一要注意的是，要尊重对方的时间。比如，如果当月你们没有什么可聊的，那就保持联系。重点不在于频繁沟通，而是在你真正遇到问题时及时伸出援手。那些乐于助人的人，只要有时间，就会欣然帮忙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tim Ferriss talks about that too. He is like, "Never ask someone to be your mentor." As you said, that's a scary proposition. You're committing to something, it's pressure versus just like, "Hey, can we just meet and can I just get some advice? And then maybe after you do that, can we meet next month also?" And just help it grow organically.
turns.zh: 蒂姆·费里斯也谈到过这个问题。他说：“永远不要要求别人做你的导师。” 正如你所说，这是一个令人却步的提议。你是在承诺某种责任，这带来了压力，而不只是说：“嘿，我们能见个面，我能得到些建议吗？” 然后或许下个月再见面聊聊。让关系自然发展。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah, definitely.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about how you develop talent and what you've learned there. But before that, I wanted to zoom out maybe first and talk about ingredients of high performance teams. So before I ask that question, can you just list the companies you work with, some of the companies you've worked with?
turns.zh: 我想谈谈你如何培养人才，以及你在这方面学到了什么。但在此之前，我想先退后一步，谈谈高效团队的构成要素。所以在问这个问题之前，你能否列出你合作过的公司，或者你曾工作过的公司？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I guess I've mentioned Dropbox. So Dropbox was my first high growth tech startup. And then after Dropbox I did a lot of advising. So I got to work with Typeform in Barcelona and then someone at Typeform introduced me to Canva. So I met Canva when they were still about 200 people in their early growth journey. Have worked with Grammarly, Miro and then I joined Webflow. And so have been fortunate to be part of a ton of, I guess what I would think are high performing teams.
turns.zh: 我想我之前提过Dropbox。Dropbox是我参与的首家高增长科技初创公司。离开Dropbox后，我做了大量顾问工作。当时我在巴塞罗那与Typeform合作，Typeform的一位高管把我介绍给了Canva。当时Canva仍处于早期发展阶段，员工规模约200人。我还与Grammarly、Miro合作过，之后加入了Webflow。能参与如此多表现卓越的团队，我深感荣幸。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 100%. That's an incredible roster. So here's the question. What are some of the most common ingredients you've seen across these teams, which from an outsider's perspective seem quite high performing?
turns.zh: 没错。这确实是一份令人惊叹的履历。那么我想问问您，在这些表现出色的团队中，您观察到的最常见的成功要素是什么？从外行视角看，这些团队的表现确实相当亮眼。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I think it first starts with the team having a really clear goals. They need to know what success looks like. And often I think that's for growth teams in particular, it's always really clear, "Hey, we need to hit certain metrics. We have certain goals for the quarter and for the year." And then also having a mission. So the mission's all about the why, right? So an example at Webflow is we have our growth team gold on ultimately the North Star is ARR, Annual Recurring Revenue. And then you break it down into the levers that drive ARR, the leading indicator, so that could be activation rates, the number of customers you bring in, et cetera. And so each team has really clear goals. And then we have our mission. The why. Our mission, the why we do it is we want to build these delightful experiences for our users. We want to support them on their journey on the product. (00:29:35): And the reason why the what is monetization is that's just a good signal that people find your product valuable, especially if they're consistently paying you and they're retaining. And then the other thing that I think is important is culture. So how are you going to do these things? When thinking about culture, obviously it depends on the function and the culture you want to set there. For me personally, the type of culture I try to set for the team is one around being really results oriented. (00:30:03): So something that someone on my team was saying the other day is you always make it really clear that we're going to be measured on impact and that's like how we are ultimately measured as a team. And so really creating that results oriented team. Also, a team that's very team first and collaborative. I think when you have very clear goals, when it's very results-oriented, you could potentially be in a situation where people feel they're competing against each other and you just don't want that. You actually want folks on the team to help each other out to share learnings. (00:30:33): I think that's what ends up being like a situation where one plus one equals three. You're not locally optimizing but you're thinking broader about the team and thinking beyond yourself. The third thing is really this ownership mentality. Something I directly saw at Dropbox is when we were a smaller company, everyone just felt a lot more ownership in accountability because there's just nobody else. You're wearing five different hats. You have to do it. (00:30:57): As you scale, it's really easy to suddenly feel like that ownership is diluted. And so something I always try to keep in the team, it's a feeling that we're owners and that really proactive mindset of how am I going to solve this problem? I'm blocked by this team, what am I going to do about it? And just being people that have strong sense of agency. And then lastly having fun. I think that especially in high pressured environments, easy to get stressed and all that stuff. And at the end of the day, this is very personal me, but the more fun you can have, the better everything is. And so just making sure you're infusing fun along the way and you're not taking things too seriously.
turns.zh:
我认为首先，团队必须有非常明确的目标。他们需要清楚成功的模样。就成长型团队而言，这一点尤为重要——目标通常十分清晰：“我们必须达成某些关键指标，本季度和本年度都有明确的目标。”此外，团队还需要有使命感。使命感关乎初衷，对吧？以Webflow为例，我们的增长团队以年度经常性收入（ARR）为核心北极星指标。然后将其拆解为推动ARR增长的关键因素，即领先指标，比如激活率、客户获取量等。每个团队都有明确的目标，接着是我们的使命——即初衷：我们要为用户打造愉悦的体验，支持他们在产品中的成长之旅。  
（00:29:35）：至于为什么以变现为核心目标，是因为这能有效衡量用户对产品的价值认可度，尤其是当用户持续付费并保持留存时。  
（00:30:03）：我认为文化建设同样重要。具体如何推进？这取决于团队职能及所需文化氛围。对我而言，我致力于打造以结果为导向的团队文化。  
（00:30:33）：团队成员曾提到，要明确传达团队将以影响力作为衡量标准，这也是我们团队的核心价值观。通过营造这种结果导向的文化，团队成员才能摒弃内部竞争，转而相互协作、分享经验。  
（00:30:57）：我认为这才是1+1大于3的秘诀。团队成员不应局限于本地优化，而应着眼于全局，突破自我局限。  
（00:31:05）：在Dropbox早期阶段，每个人都因职责交叉而具有更强的责任感。但随着规模扩大，责任感容易被稀释。因此，我始终强调团队要保持主人翁意识，主动思考问题：如何解决障碍？遇到阻碍时如何突破？始终保持行动力和主人翁精神。  
（00:31:23）：最后，保持乐趣至关重要。高压环境下容易焦虑，但适当放松能提升效率。对我个人而言，创造趣味氛围能提升整体效率。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I was taking notes as you were talking and there's kind of these four items just to summarize. One is creating a culture of impact and performance. Two is being team first and making about the team versus the person. Three is creating a sense of ownership and making people feel like they're owners and then having fun, which I love. A question I have there is say within the ownership bucket of creating a sense of ownership, what do you actually do to create that sense amongst the team?
turns.zh: 当时你在讲话时，我一直在做笔记，简单总结一下，有四点要点。第一是营造影响力和绩效导向的文化。第二是以团队为先，关注团队而非个人。第三是培养主人翁意识，让员工感受到自己是主人，然后享受工作乐趣——这一点我特别喜欢。我有个问题：在创建主人翁意识这个环节，你们具体做了哪些事来激发团队的这种意识？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I think it first starts with defining the scope that everyone is going to own and drive. So as you are setting up the team, it's important that each person on the team has scope that they can run independently and that they are excited to own and drive. So one example here is as I was leaving Dropbox, the finance team looked at our metrics and saw that each growth PM was bringing over a million in AR per year just from all the experiments.
turns.zh: 我觉得首先要明确每个成员负责的范围和自主权。当组建团队时，每个成员都需要有独立运作的自主权，并且对所负责的部分充满热情和责任感。举个例子，我离开Dropbox时，财务团队分析数据发现，每位增长型产品经理每年仅通过实验就能为公司带来超过100万美元的AR增量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Holy moly.
turns.zh: 天哪！

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah. And so that's quite a lot of impact. And being a finance team, they said logically we should just double the team. If each person brings in more than a million, if we want to double the AR, let's just double the team. And so I actually pushed back significantly though. I thought to myself, "If we double the team, what is everyone on the team going to own and drive? Is it like we split up different parts of the website, different parts of the product 1:00 PM owns just like the checkout flow. (00:32:57): I didn't think that was going to be interesting enough for the team and going to help us recruit people that were excited to solve such small parts of the growth problem. And so really thinking about how do you carve out scope and if you are a growth team, maybe thinking about splitting up by problems to solve that are really meaty by areas of the funnel like activation, monetization, et cetera. So first starting out with carving out good scope. And then the second thing is just infusing a culture of thinking like an owner. This infusing of the culture, I think it comes out in a few ways. One is, and this is really common in growth. Growth is so cross-functional that you often will end up feeling like you're blocked by other teams. (00:33:38): Let's say we want to run an experiment on this part of the product, maybe it's a core PM that kind of owns that service area that doesn't want to drive that thing or let's say or blocked by a bottleneck on designer engineering. It's something where I think if you're thinking an owner, you are not feeling easily disempowered because you can't do something and instead you're thinking, "What is everything I can do and did I exhaust all the options?" (00:34:05): And then finally it's leading by example. I try to also show to my team that I'm always thinking like an owner and then I'm always trying to do everything I can. And finally as a leader, thinking like an owner also means taking responsibility for your team. And so if things don't go right in my team, I'm the first one to say that ultimately I'm responsible and it's a failure or oversight on my side. And so that is what I think an ownership mentality is. It's just really thinking about the scope, creating that culture and then as a leader it's just seeing yourself as ultimately being accountable.
turns.zh: 是啊，这影响力确实不小。作为财务团队，他们本想简单地把团队规模翻倍。但我坚决反对。我想，如果团队规模翻倍，每个人负责的部分会被拆分得支离破碎。比如把网站的不同模块、产品中的不同功能分给不同人，比如处理结账流程的PM负责整个流程。（00:32:57）我觉得这对团队来说不够有趣，也难以吸引那些热衷于解决小问题的增长型人才。所以关键在于如何合理划分职责范围。对于增长团队来说，或许可以按漏斗阶段中的关键问题来划分，比如激活、变现等。首先要明确合理的职责范围。第二点是灌输主人翁文化。我认为这种文化可以从几个方面体现。首先，在增长团队中很常见的情况是，跨职能协作时常会遇到阻碍。比如想在产品某个模块上做实验，但产品经理不愿意推进，或者设计师遇到技术瓶颈。这时候，拥有主人翁思维的人不会轻易感到无力，而是会想：“我能做些什么？我是否已经用尽了所有可能？”（00:34:05）最后，领导者要以身作则。我努力向团队展示自己始终以主人翁身份思考问题，尽全力行动。作为领导者，拥有主人翁思维还意味着为团队负责。如果团队出现问题，我会第一个站出来承认这是我的责任和疏忽。这就是我理解的主人翁思维。关键在于清晰职责范围，培育这种文化，而作为领导者，则要始终以最终责任人自居。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And this connects to something else I wanted to pull the thread on, which is the team first bucket. I think about Meta, not to throw them under the bus or anything, but I feel like everyone I know at Meta their performance review is very tied to their impact. It's very impact driven and that leads to people needing to drive impact themselves. I drove this impact and they look at how much did you contribute to that impact versus other people on your team. And it creates some challenges I think for people. How do you create that feeling of team first, even though your performance as you talked about is so tied to here's your success metric, here's what success means for you, for the team, how do you make it feel team first versus like, I need to do this myself?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这也正好让我能顺便谈谈另一个话题——团队至上理念。我以Meta为例——不是要批评他们，而是我发现身边所有Meta员工的绩效评估都与他们的影响力挂钩。这是一种以影响力为导向的考核体系，导致人们不得不主动去创造影响力。我就曾亲身经历过这样的考核：公司会衡量你对团队整体影响力的贡献程度，并将其与团队其他成员进行比较。这种机制确实给员工带来了挑战。尽管你提到的绩效衡量标准是个人成就，但团队至上理念又如何能真正落地？当你被问到“你对团队的贡献有多大”时，如何让人们感受到“团队优先”的价值？而不是陷入“我必须自己达成目标”的困境？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: There's definitely a delicate balance here. It comes down to the way that I think the manager leads the team and sets the tone. And so for me, I always make it clear that even though results are important, it's a team sport. And so I often find that I am encouraging the team to work together. So again, as a leader, you have context in everything happening. So sometimes I know 1:00 PM is working on something or even a PM outside our team is working on something and I try to actually fill in context if I think someone on my team could contribute. And I encourage that action even though it doesn't maybe feed into impact on the thing they're driving. So it really comes down to the culture that you set and what you encourage the team to do. I also think the more that you can see that you actually benefit from helping each other out, the better it is. (00:36:15): And finally, I think again, leading by example, because I actually am very team first, I'm often actually helping other teams and doing things that might not ultimately benefit or be part of my scope. A good example here is I was actually driving pricing and packaging at Webflow for a very long time just because no one at the company was driving it and it was a huge opportunity area and I actually was doing it for enterprise pricing too. And so even though I am overseeing self-serve, I was actually supporting enterprise pricing and packaging. And so I also showed to my team, "Hey, I'm also doing all these things to help the company." And I think that is what helps set that tone and that culture.
turns.zh: 这确实需要找到一个微妙的平衡点。关键在于管理者如何引领团队，如何设定正确的价值观。对我来说，始终强调结果固然重要，但这毕竟是团队协作的游戏。因此，我会经常鼓励团队成员相互协作。作为领导者，你需要洞察全局。比如，我会注意到下午1点团队在忙什么，甚至其他团队成员在忙什么项目。若我认为团队成员能参与其中，就会主动补充信息。即便这些工作与他们主导的项目无关，我也会积极推动。这最终取决于你所营造的文化氛围，以及你如何引导团队行动。我相信，当人们切实感受到互助带来的价值时，文化建设才能真正落地生根。（00:36:15）最后，以身作则至关重要。作为一个始终以团队为先的人，我经常帮助其他团队完成超出职责范围的工作——比如在Webflow，我长期负责定价和包装模块的开发，尽管公司里没人负责这个领域，但这是一个巨大的机遇。我甚至还为企业级定价提供支持。虽然我主要负责自助服务业务，但我也会为企业级定价和包装模块提供支持。通过这种示范，我向团队传递了这样的信息：“嘿，我也在为公司做这些事情。”我认为这正是树立团队文化的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you then avoid doing too much work? I think there's also this challenge of people being too good at too many things and then they end up doing so many things and then they burn out. Do you have any rules of thumb or lessons there?
turns.zh: 那如何避免过度加班呢？我觉得还有一个挑战是，人们往往擅长太多事情，结果却身兼数职，直至精疲力竭。对此你有什么经验或建议吗？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I think for me it's been a learning journey too. I've actually gotten feedback on that very thing for my team that Melissa sometimes taking on too much or trying to do too much. And so I think it's a delicate balance. If we're talking about that person individually, you have to know what your limits are and you also can do things in spurts, but it's important to know ultimately what you can take on. Also I find that putting a specific timeline like, "Hey, I'm going to do this thing for a quarter, but after that we really need to find somebody else to do it." Or hand it off is really helpful. It's definitely a delicate balance. I do think it's a great question because I think that's a common thing people early in their careers struggle with, which is they could lose focus because they're trying to help everybody. (00:37:49): That was actually a problem I had when I first joined Dropbox is I was the only sales ops person, so I was just helping every sales leader with their metrics and very focused. And so it is a little bit of trial and error. I think the most important thing is to not be so overly focused on just what you're doing and try to help others, but then knowing that there are certain things that just can't drop. And if you start to see things that are starting to drop that you're ultimately responsible for, that's a signal that you're taking on too much.
turns.zh:
我觉得对我来说，这也是一个学习的过程。实际上，我团队里有人就曾反馈过，梅丽莎有时会揽下太多工作，或者试图做得太多。所以我认为这是一个微妙的平衡。如果从个人层面来讲，你必须清楚自己的极限所在，你也可以分阶段完成任务，但最重要的是要清楚自己能承受多少。另外，我发现设定一个具体的时间节点很有帮助，比如“我会在这个季度负责这项工作，但之后我们真的需要找其他人来接手。”或者将任务移交给其他人，这真的很有用。总之，这是一个需要平衡的微妙问题。我认为这是一个很好的问题，因为我认为这是初入职场的人常遇到的困境——他们可能会因为试图帮助每个人而失去专注力。

（00:37:49）：这实际上是我刚加入Dropbox时遇到的一个问题，当时我是唯一的销售运营人员，所以我只专注于帮助每个销售主管处理他们的指标。这确实需要不断尝试和摸索。我认为最重要的是不要过度专注于自己正在做的事情，而是尽力帮助他人，但同时要知道有些事情是不可放手的。如果你开始发现自己负责的某些事情出现问题，说明你承担了太多工作。

turns.zh:
