（00:39:25）：让我们回到培养人才这个话题。我之前有点跑题了，但我想回到这个话题上。我们讨论了你对培养人才的热情，以及你所经历的好处。我很好奇你实际做了什么来帮助人们成为更好的产品经理、各类领导者。你见过哪些有效的方法？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: In terms of developing talent, I think of this as stages of the life cycle of your relationship, right? So I think at first actually starts is a very meta as a growth person starts with when you hire somebody, really making sure you're finding somebody that is a good fit for the role. It's a good mutual fit. I also tend to look for folks that have a growth mindset. (00:40:06): There're people that are wanting to learn. They're looking for feedback. They take feedback well. And then after that they join the company, and as a manager, my job is to help set them up for success. So how do I ramp them up as quickly as possible, connect them to the right people, the company? How do I also make sure it's clear what success looks like in their first 90 days? And then how do I help them secure early wins essentially? (00:40:32): So I often will suggest, "Hey, you should do this presentation. It's a great way to get visibility early in your journey here." Here are some things where there's low hanging fruit or even rotting fruit that you should take on into secure early wins. Then in your journey, I think it's a lot about just giving feedback along the way, making sure you give visibility. One recent hack I have is having folks on the team create looms that they can share with different leaders at Webflow. It's hard to sometimes get visibility and get live meeting calendars, but if you create a five or 10 minute-loom on something you did. That's just a great way to get visibility. (00:41:10): And then finally, I think it's that lifelong relationship actually. So I'm still in touch with a lot of people that I've managed and I've helped them. Whether it's looking for their new job or they have career advice, I always make myself available. And so it's actually that lifelong journey of just developing that person. And at some point it's not even developing that person, but it's having a friendship with somebody. And I feel like I've learned a ton from people that I have managed. And so it ends up being this really great thing where you initially started working together but you now know each other so well. And I think that's even how I've developed as a manager is just getting feedback from my team.
turns.zh: 谈到人才培养，我认为这就像是你们关系生命周期的不同阶段，对吧？所以我认为首先实际上是从一个很宏观的角度开始的，当你招聘某个人时，要确保找到真正适合这个角色的人。这是一个良好的双向匹配。我还倾向于寻找具有成长型思维的人（00:40:06）：有些人渴望学习。他们乐于接受反馈，并且能很好地处理反馈。然后他们加入公司后，作为管理者，我的职责就是帮助他们为成功做好准备。那么如何尽快让他们适应环境，让他们与公司和合适的人建立联系？如何在他们入职的前90天就明确成功的标准？然后如何帮助他们尽早取得成功？（00:40:32）：所以我经常会建议：“嘿，你应该做这个演示。这是在你职业生涯初期获得关注的绝佳方式。” 这里有一些低风险甚至是容易出成果的事情，你应该抓住机会取得早期成功。然后在他们的职业发展过程中，我认为关键在于持续提供反馈，确保他们获得关注。最近我发现一个妙招，就是让团队成员制作Loom视频，分享给Webflow的不同领导。有些时候很难获得关注和安排会议日程，但如果你制作一个五到十分钟的Loom视频，展示自己做过的事情，这就是获取关注的绝佳方式。（00:41:10）：最后， 我认为这实际上是一段终身的关系。所以我至今仍与许多我管理过并帮助过的人保持联系。无论是他们寻找新工作还是寻求职业建议，我都会尽力提供帮助。这实际上是一段终身的旅程，就是培养那个人。在某个阶段，这甚至不再是培养一个人，而是与某人建立友谊。我觉得我从我管理过的人身上学到了很多东西。最终，你们最初只是在一起工作，但现在你们非常了解彼此。我认为这就是我成长为一名管理者的秘诀——不断从团队中获得反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This all comes back to something you mentioned a couple of times earlier, just caring a lot about the person that you work with. Your approach also reminds me of this book, Radical Candor. I imagine you're a fan and that's kind of the way you think about it.
turns.zh: 这一切都回到了你之前多次提到的一点，那就是非常关心与你共事的人。你的方法也让我想起了《Radical Candor》这本书。我猜你一定是这本书的粉丝，这也正是你思考问题的方式。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah, definitely. Interestingly enough, Kim Scott was at Dropbox for a short period of time, so when I joined Dropbox, she was actually on my interview panel and we overlapped for three months and she actually workshopped that book with our team before she published it. And that always resonated with me. And I remember her saying you have to ... I forget the exact words, but it's essentially be direct but deeply care.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对如此。有趣的是，金·斯科特曾在Dropbox短暂任职，所以当我加入Dropbox时，她实际上在我的面试小组中，我们共事了三个月，她甚至在出版这本书前就与我们的团队一起进行了研讨。这让我深有共鸣。我记得她说过你必须……我记不清具体措辞了，但本质上就是要直言不讳但真心关怀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Care deeply, but something directly challenged directly. Something like that.
turns.zh: 是的。要真心关怀，但也要直言不讳地提出挑战。类似这样的。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah, care deeply but challenge directly and that has always been something that is something I try to infuse and has really inspired me as leader.
turns.zh: 是的，真心关怀但直言不讳地提出挑战，这一直是我努力贯彻的理念，也深深启发了我作为领导者的成长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We're going to link to that book if folks don't know about it. I love it. You talked about hiring PMs and how that is important in building high performing teams. So let's spend a little time there, maybe just two questions all throughout and you can approach them however you want. One is just what do you look for when you're hiring product managers? You've hired a lot of PMs. You've managed a lot of PMs over the years. What do you look for, especially things that maybe other people don't focus on enough, and then just what is your interview process? What do you find is most helpful for interviewing process-wise?
turns.zh: 太棒了。如果大家还不了解这本书，我们会附上链接。我超爱它。你之前谈到招聘产品经理的重要性，以及如何组建高效团队。咱们就来深入探讨一下吧，或许先抛出两个问题，大家可以自由发挥。第一个问题是：招聘产品经理时，你最看重哪些方面？你招过很多产品经理，多年来也管理过不少。能否分享一些其他人可能不太关注的关键点？第二个问题：你的面试流程是怎样的？在面试过程中，有哪些方法最为有效？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: In terms of what I look for, I think there's this kind of known list of things that you probably want to look for, for a PM that I probably are not going to ... I'm say anything groundbreaking here, but obviously communication skills, the ability to manage stakeholders and work well cross-functionally. The things that I lean especially heavy on in my interview process is this concept of first principles thinking or strong critical thinking. So usually there's some live problem solving component to my interview process where I really lean more heavily into how would you approach X problem? And then I dig into the Y and try to understand why would they approach it this way, see what questions they're asking and just see how they approach problem solving. (00:43:55): And then the other thing that I look for that I mentioned is that growth mindset. So really seeing how does this person take feedback. And so I'll actually sometimes give feedback to candidates through the process. Something that I do that I learned a few years ago that was super helpful, so I always have a presentation component to the interview process that checks for prepared thinking communication. And I recommend a prep call between the two of us before that presentation. And I actually will give feedback on the presentation. (00:44:26): And what this gives me signal is what is it actually going to be like to work together? And then I see how they incorporate it into the final product and that is always really interesting and sometimes it's the biggest signal to what it's going to be like to work with this person.
turns.zh: 关于招聘标准，我觉得有一些公认的要素，比如沟通能力、协调利益相关者及跨部门协作的能力。但我更关注面试中的两个核心点：第一原则思维和批判性思考。在面试中，我通常会加入实时解决问题的环节，深入探讨候选人如何处理某个问题。然后我会追问他们为何采用这种方法，观察他们的提问思路和解决问题的逻辑。（00:43:55）另外，我特别看重成长型思维，观察候选人如何接受反馈。实际上，面试过程中我也会给予反馈。几年前我总结的一个有效方法是，在面试前安排一场演示环节，用来评估候选人的思维准备和沟通能力。我建议双方在演示前进行预沟通，并在演示后提供反馈。通过这种方式，我能预判与候选人共事的真实场景，并观察他们如何将所学融入最终成果，这往往能最直接地反映出与他们合作的效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, this is great. I want to spend a little time here. So what is the actual sequence that you recommend or you use for interviewing? There's a presentation, there's a rep call but also is kind of involved in that.
turns.zh: 好的，非常感谢。接下来我想深入探讨一下具体的面试流程。您提到的环节包括演示和反馈电话，但具体顺序如何呢？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Usually hiring manager screen, and I actually do the live problem solving at this screen. I actually think it weeds out the most people. And there's actually two things I do here. One is a live problem solving. How would you approach X? So let's say I'm hiring for pricing at Webflow, I would ask, "How would you approach pricing?" I sometimes would say, "Hey, do you have your laptop? Can you pull up our pricing page? Curious to get your thoughts, what would you want to change?" That was a trick I learned at Dropbox where we would actually pull up the Dropbox website and be like, "Hey, what'd you want to test here? Why?" And you get a ton of signal on how they approach the problem, how they think. (00:45:25): I ask why a bunch. And then the next screen is talking to more folks at the team that test for different competencies. And depending on what you're hiring for, we just have each person focused on a different competency. And it also depends on the roles. So some roles are more technical, some require working more closely with different stakeholders, so you want to make sure you can test those things. And then the final round is the presentation and then also maybe a conversation on other areas. (00:45:52): We want that kind of come through the interview process. We want to dig in further. The presentation is usually thinking through how you'd approach, your collecting all this information on the company or the problem throughout the interview process. And so it culminates in what do you think this should look like or maybe what would you want to do in your first 90 days? It depends on the role, but it's usually some type of presentation about the problem you would be working on at the company. (00:46:18): Before that, we have that preparation call with me where often candidates will have questions like, "Oh, I need to know this data," or "I'm curious about X." And so it's really just a call to help them. And then at this stage too, they'll often have the actual draft of the presentation and so we'll go through it together and I'll actually be like, "Hey, I think you should lean in heavier here. How would you think about this?" I'll even say for example, at Webflow I'll be like, "We're thinking about X, Y, Z thing just so you know. And maybe incorporating that into your presentation would be really helpful. (00:46:50): And so that's where I get a lot of signal of what is it going to be like to work with this person on a presentation? And then I'll see in the presentation whether they incorporate it or not or how they did. And sometimes I've seen candidates that didn't incorporate any of it and I kind of am like, "Okay, this is probably not a fit." And actually I think that other thing about that call is it helps just set the candidate up for success. It's actually quite a lot of work to create a presentation. The more we can help them by giving them information, making sure they can be successful, it's helpful. And I think guess lastly, it gives them a taste of what it's like to work with me.
turns.zh: 通常，招聘经理会进行初步筛选，而我实际上会在这个环节进行现场问题解决。我认为这个环节能筛选掉最多不合适的人选。具体来说，我在这里会做两件事。第一是现场解决问题。比如说，如果我在Webflow招聘定价岗位，我会问：“你会如何着手定价？”有时我会说：“嘿，你带电脑了吗？能打开我们的定价页面吗？想听听你的想法，你希望做出哪些改进？”这是我在Dropbox学到的技巧——我们会直接打开Dropbox官网，问对方：“你想在这里测试什么？为什么？”通过这种方式，能深入了解候选人解决问题的方式和思维模式。（00:45:25）我会反复追问原因。接下来是与团队其他成员交流的环节，根据招聘职位不同，我们会安排不同成员专注于不同能力的测试。不同职位的侧重点也不同——有些职位更偏技术性，有些则需要与不同利益相关者密切合作，因此必须确保能测试到这些能力。最后一轮是面试演示，可能还会有其他环节的讨论。（00:45:52）我们希望通过整个面试流程深入了解候选人。演示环节通常需要回顾整个面试过程中收集的信息，比如公司背景、项目挑战等。最终会讨论你认为应如何设计方案，或在入职前90天内会优先开展哪些工作。（00:46:18）在此之前，我们会进行准备沟通，候选人常会提出诸如“我需要了解这些数据”、“我对X很感兴趣”等问题。这个环节主要是帮助他们准备。演示环节中，他们通常会带着初稿，我们会一起分析，我会说：“你可以再深入些。”比如在Webflow，我会说：“我们正在考虑X、Y、Z事宜，供你参考。把这些融入你的演示会很有帮助。”通过此环节，我能判断候选人是否能与我高效合作。最后，我会根据演示效果判断是否适合录用。我认为这个沟通环节还有助于候选人为成功做好准备。制作演示稿需要大量工作，能提供信息支持、确保成功完成，这非常有帮助。最后，我想说这让候选人提前体验了与我共事的感觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've never heard of that step before. That is really interesting. They actually give them feedback before they present. I imagine they're like, "What the hell is going on here?" I thought I was trying to show them what I can do, not like they're going to help me do a great job. That is really interesting. Maybe two very logistical questions there. How much time do you give them to work on this presentation? And then two, you said that you asked some questions related to the actual problem solving versus a theoretical problem. So those are the two questions, I guess.
turns.zh: 我之前从未听说过这一步骤。这真的很有趣。他们实际上会在演示前给出反馈。我能想象他们当时会想：“这到底是怎么回事？”我原以为自己是在向他们展示我的能力，而不是指望他们能帮我把工作做得更出色。这确实很有趣。可能有两个比较实际的问题。第一，您给他们多长时间准备这份演示？第二，您提到会问一些与实际问题解决相关的而非理论性的问题。以上就是我的两个问题。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Typically we will schedule it about a week in advance. They have a week. The tricky thing here is obviously it's a big ask to ask someone to create a presentation. And so if it's one week that's long enough to create it, but it's short enough that you don't spend tons of time. The other thing is just making it clear, don't exceed more than X number of slides. In Webflow's case we've done, don't exceed more than 30 slides. And that's like quite a lot. We do not expect you to do 30 slides. And then the other thing I make sure to emphasize is it's really about wanting to know how you'd approach it. So don't worry about the slides, be able to talk to it and have what you need to talk to it because we're actually just looking for the substance. And so that's how much time we give them and it's usually a 30-minute presentation with 15-minute Q&A. (00:48:42): The second part of your question was, so in terms of picking the topic, so there's a few ways to think about it. I know some folks will be like, "Oh, we have candidates present on something they've worked with in the past." I've tried that form and it's really difficult because I found that candidates even sometimes spend tons of time sharing the context of that company. And then also it doesn't really give a sense of, because as you're interviewing from a role, you're getting a ton of context on the actual company and the problem. And so it also is testing for how much did they pick up along the way. Also, would they like working on this area once they join? So there are some candidates that sometimes are concerned about the amount of time they would spend on it or say, "This is going to be a big lift." (00:49:30): And definitely mindful of that. I think the main thing though is it is actually in the candidate's best interest to kind of understand what they're going to work on and start to understand,
turns.zh: 通常我们会提前一周安排相关事宜。他们有一周的时间准备。关键在于，要求别人制作演示文件确实是个不小的挑战。因此，如果给一周时间既足够他们完成，又不会让他们耗费过多精力。另外，我们会明确规定幻灯片数量不得超过X页。以Webflow为例，我们设定上限为30页，这已经算很多了。我们并不期望他们制作30页幻灯片。最重要的是，我会强调重点在于想了解他们如何处理问题。所以不必过于在意幻灯片部分，关键是能流畅地阐述思路并具备相关知识。这就是我们分配的时间安排，通常30分钟演示，15分钟问答环节。（00:48:42）：您问题的第二部分是关于选题的。有几种思路可以考虑。我知道有些公司会让候选人展示他们过去参与过的项目。但这种形式效果不佳，因为候选人往往会花大量时间分享原公司的背景信息。同时，招聘者通过面试已获取了大量关于目标公司和实际问题的信息。这也需要测试他们在项目中的学习能力，以及他们加入后是否愿意从事这方面工作。有些候选人会担心投入过多时间，或者认为这会是个巨大的挑战。对此我们必须留意。最重要的是，深入了解未来工作内容对候选人自身有利。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: For example, there are some candidates that have gone through the far through process and haven't worked in the Webflow product very much. And I always think that's an interesting flag because if you aren't in the product a lot, you're not going to get good context on whether you like it or not. And so I actually think it's almost even in the best interest of the candidate to go much deeper.
turns.zh: 例如，有些候选人经历了漫长的面试流程，却对Webflow产品知之甚少。我认为这是一个危险信号，因为如果对产品不熟悉，就无法准确判断是否喜欢这份工作。因此，我认为深入了解产品特性对候选人更有益处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could spend another hour talking about interview strategy, but I want to make sure we have time for the growth team stuff. So let's transition to that. And my first question here is you've worked with a lot of different teams, a lot of different companies on helping them figure out their growth strategy, hiring their growth teams, just kind of figuring out growth. I'm curious what the most common pitfalls and mistakes you've seen across companies trying to figure out growth and build growth teams.
turns.zh: 我可以再花一个小时讨论面试策略，但现在要转到增长团队相关话题了。首先，您与许多不同团队和公司合作过，帮助他们制定增长策略、组建增长团队、探索增长模式。我很好奇在帮助企业制定增长策略和组建增长团队过程中，您见过最常见的陷阱和错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: One of the most common pitfalls I'd say is not having, and I've alluded to this, not having a sense of the big picture from the start and not being strategic about what your go-to market strategy is going to be. Also, what is your pricing and packaging going to look like? So I wrote actually an article for the YC blog a few years ago with Abby [inaudible 00:50:48] who was on my team at Dropbox about this because I felt like even at Dropbox, I mean it's a great thing. We were haphazardly finding amazing things. We had a freemium consumer product. Then we realized people wanted a Teams product, so we built a Teams product, but we never created that whole blueprint of what should it look like and what are the different connection points across consumer business? What should our model look like? I've also seen companies that maybe weren't intentional enough about pricing from the start, and so thinking about what is the value metric? (00:51:20): And then they've already have massive scale and then they're rethinking their pricing. That's actually quite a big headache to actually think about, okay, how do we grandfather users? How do we bring the legacy customers onto our new pricing? And so thinking about your pricing from the start is important thing might go to market from the start is important. The other thing I have seen a lot is just like, again, this goes back to learning from Dropbox is the execution folks taking a class or reading a lot about growth and trying to do the same thing and not really actually starting from first let's look at our data. Let's talk to our customers. What do we think are the biggest hypotheses? And starting your experiments based on your own data and right-sizing the experiment. (00:52:10): I think sometimes teams are experimenting on things that are too small, that aren't going to move the needle because they heard it was really successful company X, but that company X might be a Dropbox where every 0.5% improvement in conversion makes a difference, but if you're early stage doesn't matter and you need to actually think bigger. The other thing is the opposite problem, redoing a whole thing but not having a hypothesis, this was an early mistake I made at Dropbox where I redid the checkout page to something that I thought was better UX, but then I changed so many different components that even when it failed, it was unclear why it failed. So really distilling it to hypotheses. (00:52:48): And then the last thing I would say is figuring out what I call the flying formation of how the different growth teams will work with other companies. And again, I alluded to this, but growth shouldn't feel like it's a layer on top. And a lot of the things that are tricky early on is figuring out how you work with other teams. I think the best or the ideal way to work is to have growth infuse in the company. And so an example here is often the growth team is going to be potentially the closest to the user. (00:53:21): They're going to get a lot of feedback. They're going to hear directly from the user. As a growth team, I think one of the big values that we can have is actually giving that feedback back to other teams at the company. And so even as a growth team, can we help inform the product roadmap? Also on the reverse, thinking about as PMs, how can PMs be more growth oriented as well?
turns.zh:
我认为最常见的陷阱之一，是从一开始就缺乏大局观，缺乏战略性思考，未能制定清晰的市场推广策略。此外，你的定价和产品包装又该如何设计？几年前，我曾与Abby（在Dropbox时曾是我的团队成员）为YC博客撰写了一篇相关文章，因为我发现即使在Dropbox内部，虽然我们偶然发现了许多惊喜产品，但我们仍未能构建完整的蓝图——如何衔接消费者与企业业务？定价模式又该如何设计？我还见过许多公司从一开始就未能充分考虑定价策略。例如，他们在产品已形成大规模后才重新审视定价，这无疑是个令人头疼的难题。如何保留老用户？如何将遗留客户过渡到新定价体系？因此，从一开始就规划定价策略至关重要。

另一个常见问题是——这又回到了Dropbox的经验——许多团队盲目模仿成功案例，却未能从实际出发。例如，他们先是参加增长课程、大量阅读相关书籍，随后照搬策略，却从未真正审视自身数据、倾听用户需求、梳理核心假设，并基于数据优化实验规模。这类错误往往源于两个极端：要么尝试微不足道的改进，要么因规模过大而束手束脚。

另一个反面教训是——这也与Dropbox早期经历相呼应——在未形成假设前就重构产品。例如，我曾将结账页面改版为更美观的界面，但由于改动过多，最终以失败告终，却难以总结原因。因此，关键在于提炼核心假设。

最后，我想强调的是构建增长团队的协作机制。增长团队不应成为独立层级，而是应深度融入产品研发。例如，增长团队通常最贴近用户，能直接获取反馈。作为增长团队，我们能否为产品路线图提供决策依据？反之，产品经理又如何能更主动地融入增长思维？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like this term flying formation. I've never heard of this before. What is that exactly again? Is that just how growth is integrated within the company?
turns.zh: 我喜欢“飞行编队”这个术语。之前从没听过这个词。能再详细解释一下吗？这到底是什么意思？难道就是指公司内部如何整合各团队的协作吗？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah, I guess flying formation essentially, I don't know where it comes from. I guess maybe it's a military term or something. Your finger.
turns.zh: 是啊，我猜“飞行编队”本质上……我不知道它源自哪里。可能是个军事术语之类的。你的手指。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can say that. Yeah, like the Blue Angels
turns.zh: 我可以这么说。对，就像“蓝天使飞行队”那样。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Work together?
turns.zh: 一起合作？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah. I think of flying formation as how do we work together across teams. You also can think of it as a DACI too, driver accountable, contribute informed. I think sometimes when you don't know how you're going to work together, you end up stepping over each other's toes. You're unclear. Who was the decision maker here? Who did we need to work with? At what point in the journey? And so the flying formation, what I think it is, is part of it is a DACI of what are the different roles?
turns.zh: 对。我把“飞行编队”理解为团队间如何协同合作。你也可以把它看作DACI框架——驱动者（Driver）、责任人（Accountable）、贡献者（Contributor）和知情者（Informed）。有时候当你不清楚如何协作时，往往会互相扯皮，职责不清。比如决策者是谁？需要与哪些团队合作？在项目的哪个阶段？所以“飞行编队”在我看来，部分体现了DACI框架，即不同角色的职责分工。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you define that actually? Because a lot of people probably won't know that term.
turns.zh: 能具体解释一下吗？因为很多人可能不熟悉这个术语。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: A DACI is a framework to think about the different roles on the team on a project or an area. So D stands for Driver. This is the person driving the project. A is Accountable, this is the person that's ultimately accountable and is often the final decision maker if there's any open questions. C is Contributor, these are all the different teams that are going to contribute. And then I is informed. These are the people that need to be informed, but they're not directly contributing. They're not a decision maker and part of the project. (00:55:08): And so it's a nice simple framework for when you are working across teams and it needs to be clear who is in what role. And the area that tends to be the most confusing can be the accountable and who the decision maker is. It can be easy to have lots of teams and then it's unclear how do we get to a decision ultimately and who should make that decision. And that person should often be the person that has the most context or is ultimately responsible. (00:55:33): And so I think the flying formation has this DACI. I often also put operating rhythms in it, so it's clear what is happening at what point. And so we created a flying formation when we were first starting the growth team at Webflow and we were trying to figure out how does product growth work with product, how does product growth work with growth marketing? What are the different cadences that each team has? And so very tactically we put a doc together to say, okay, product growth is accountable for all the metrics downstream of signups. Growth marketing is accountable for signups. They're also driving or have goals around CAC, their customer acquisition costs, and these are the different metrics everyone owns. (00:56:14): We have a weekly meeting where we look at the metrics together. We also will do updates around the room to talk about initiatives and identify areas we want to work with. And then we also think through quarterly planning where we're each identifying projects that we're driving. There's some projects that we might also work on together. And so it's essentially that meeting cadence that you're going to have the operating rhythms. That's essentially how I think about a flying formation.
turns.zh: DACI是一个思考团队或项目中不同角色的框架。D代表驱动者（Driver），负责项目推进；A是责任人（Accountable），通常是最终决策者；C是贡献者（Contributor），即各团队成员；I是知情者（Informed），需要了解进展但不直接参与决策。（00:55:08）这个框架在跨团队协作时很实用，能明确各成员的角色。最容易混淆的部分是责任归属和决策者角色。多个团队协作时，决策流程不清晰，责任分工模糊。通常，拥有最多背景信息或最终责任的人应成为决策者。（00:55:33）我们在Webflow成立增长团队时，就构建了飞行编队框架，理清了产品增长与增长营销的协作流程，明确了各团队的周期节点。每周我们会一起复盘数据，每季度规划项目进展，必要时跨团队合作。这种定期会议机制正是飞行编队的核心运作机制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. That would make a great blog post. By the way, if you're looking for something to write an example of your actual client formation Webflow, I think people would love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。这会是一篇很棒的博客文章。顺便说一句，如果你想写一篇关于你实际客户获取案例的博文，特别是用Webflow实现的，我想人们会很感兴趣的。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One kind of tangent that I wanted to touch on is there's this trend of product teams owning revenue. Elena talked about this on a recent podcast. You have a perspective on should product growth teams own revenue and have revenue numbers as their goals or not?
turns.zh: 我还想提一个相关话题，就是产品团队自主负责营收的趋势。埃琳娜在最近的一期播客中提到了这个问题。你对产品增长团队是否应该自主负责营收并以营收数字为目标有何看法？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah, really it depends on the company and what product growth is driving. I've always, in the companies I was at and actually even the companies I advise, the product growth team owns revenue, so it's not always the case. I've actually seen revenue owned by marketing. So marketing makes sense if it's more top of funnel growth. I've also seen it, this is an interesting one, by finance actually. This is usually early in the company. (00:57:31): So early at Canva, it was owned by finance and that's because finance had a view on everything happening in the business and would actually be maybe advising other teams on, "Hey, our conversion rates could improve, we need to do X." Or we're not driving signups and customers efficiently, but over time it doesn't really sit in finance. That has evolved and then now sits under the person that is driving product growth in product. So I have seen it more often than not being owned by product. Our team at Dropbox moved a ton actually. We started marketing. We actually then report into the revenue org with sales, and then we finally moved into product because we realized so much of our revenue was that product growth motion happening in the product that we felt it was important that that product team owned revenue.
turns.zh: 嗯，这实际上取决于公司的情况以及产品增长所推动的业务方向。在我曾任职的公司，甚至是我为其提供咨询的公司，产品增长团队通常负责营收，但这并非普遍情况。实际上我见过营收由市场部门负责的情况。如果是漏斗顶端的增长，这对市场部门来说是合理的。我还见过由财务部门负责营收的情况，尤其是在公司初期阶段。（00:57:31）：比如Canva早期阶段，营收由财务部门负责，因为财务部门能洞察公司业务的全局，可能会给其他团队建议，比如“我们的转化率可以提升，需要采取X措施”，或者“我们没有有效获取新用户和客户”等。但随着公司发展，这部分职责逐渐转移到产品增长团队手中。Dropbox的团队就经历过多次调整。我们最初做市场工作，后来将报告线移交给销售团队，最终又转回产品团队，因为我们意识到营收很大程度上源于产品增长流程，因此让产品团队负责营收至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of the things you're talking about are based in how growth starts at a company. I imagine one of the most common questions you get is, how do I start to invest in growth? How do I hire my first growth person? How do I build a team around them? It's one of the most common questions I get. So let's spend a little time here. What is your advice to founders that are just starting to think about building their initial growth team and how to approach that to look for initially and kind of think about that longer term?
turns.zh: 你提到的很多内容都基于增长在公司中的起步阶段。我想你最常被问到的问题之一是：如何开始投资增长？如何招聘首位增长团队成员？如何围绕他们组建团队？这确实是我最常被问到的问题之一。接下来我们花点时间探讨这个问题。对于刚开始考虑组建初期增长团队的创始人，你有什么建议？如何着手组建团队，如何寻找合适人才，以及如何从长远角度规划？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I get this question a lot as well. I'd say initially when a company's starting out, the goal is getting to product market fit and figuring out who their ideal customer profile is, like their ICP. And at this point, I think everyone at the company should be thinking about growth. They're finding their first few design partners that they will co-create the product with. They're figuring out who is their product resonating with, who is maybe also the decision maker in purchasing the product. And they're figuring out, do we want kind of a bottom up product led motion? Are we going to lean more heavily into sales? Are we going to do both? (00:59:18): After you reach product market fit and you're starting to get your first few customers, the first growth per person I see more often than not isn't someone driving acquisition. You need to find your first a thousand or thousands of customers and you need to do it at scale. And so if that is the focus of the company, typically what I would recommend is somebody that they don't need to be an expert, but ideally they understand maybe one or two channels well and that they're the channels that you have hypothesis, you will find traction in. (00:59:50): And I see this person a little bit like a portfolio manager, right? Because you're trying to figure out ... Usually companies don't have many channels that are split evenly. They find one or two that really work and make up like it's 80/20 rule. It makes us up 80% of where the signups are coming from and this portfolio manager is testing different things out. Even you could leverage agencies. There are a lot of agencies out there for SEO, for paid marketing, et cetera, but they are smart enough to define, is this working? How do I do it at scale? You also want to make sure it's quality signups that are actually monetizable. (01:00:24): And so that is a role typically if you're hiring an acquisition of that first growth person. And then the other two areas to focus early on, but I don't think you need a dedicated person for are activation. You want to make sure as you're pouring leads into the top of funnel, you're activating users. And here I don't think you actually need to do AB testing. Your volume isn't probably going to be strong enough. I think even just finding five individuals that are part of your target audience, just doing user testing, set up a Zoom, watch them onboard onto the product and have them talk out loud. You'll fight a lot and you can also just take best practices of onboarding checklists, et cetera. So activation and then I've said this a lot, but pricing and packaging, really thinking about pricing, but I don't think that needs to be a dedicated person.
turns.zh:
我也经常被问到这个问题。我想说，在公司初创阶段，目标是实现产品与市场的匹配，明确理想客户画像，比如ICP（理想客户画像）。这个阶段，我认为公司里的每个人都应该关注增长。他们会寻找最初的几位设计合作伙伴，共同打造产品。他们会研究产品在哪些人群中产生共鸣，哪些人群可能也是购买决策者。同时，他们需要思考：是采取自下而上的产品主导策略？还是更倾向于销售驱动？或者两者兼顾？（00:59:18）：当产品与市场实现匹配，开始获得首批客户后，最常见的增长策略并非单纯依赖收购客户。你需要找到首批千位或数千位客户，并且要大规模地完成这一目标。因此，如果这是公司的核心关注点，我通常建议聘请一个不必是专家，但最好对一两个渠道有深入理解的人——这些渠道正是你假设能带来转化的地方。（00:59:50）：我把这个角色想象成投资组合经理，因为你需要不断探索……通常公司不会有多个均衡分配的渠道。他们会找到一两个真正有效的渠道，并遵循80/20法则。这些渠道可能占到注册用户的80%，而这位投资组合经理会不断测试不同方案。甚至可以借助代理机构。市场上有很多SEO、付费营销等服务机构，但关键在于他们要善于评估：这个方案是否有效？如何实现规模化？同时要确保这些优质注册用户确实具有变现潜力。
（01:00:24）：这就是招聘首位增长团队成员的核心职责。另外两个早期关注点是激活用户。虽然不需要专人负责，但需要确保在不断引入潜在客户时，能有效激活用户。这里无需AB测试，初期数据量不足以支撑测试。只需找到5位目标受众，进行用户测试，组织Zoom会议，观察他们上手产品过程，并收集最佳实践即可。至于定价和包装策略，我常强调要深入思考定价策略，但无需专人负责。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What kind of profile have you found to be most successful for this sort of person? Some people will look for like, I want to hire Melissa and let's just go big. The best person I can find and have them own this versus someone that's just new from school that's going to figure it out and I guess they're somewhere in the middle. What do you find that's best for that first hire?
turns.zh: 对于这类职位，你认为最成功的候选人是什么样的？有些人会说：我想聘请梅丽莎，直接放手让他们全权负责。另一些人则认为：找个刚毕业的新人来摸索，应该更稳妥。理想情况是两者折中。但对于首位增长团队成员，你认为怎样的配置最合适？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: It really depends on the current makeup of the team. How much do the founders themselves or the current team, how much of an interest do they have in growth? If they have an interest in growth and it's more about finding someone to execute, I think it's finding someone that's a bit earlier in their career potentially that is just a strong first principles thinker. I think there's hit or miss on, I'm a former consultant, so I used to always say find a former consultant. I do think there can be hit or miss and there is some value in folks that actually understand acquisition and have done it before and so maybe have figured out certain channels. (01:02:04): So I think you either go for someone that's done acquisition before, maybe they're a little bit early in their career, so they have this great growth mindset, but make sure they're a first principles thinker. The other option is find just a really smart person early in their career, have them take up Reforge class, have them soak up everything, and then the other option of hiring someone more experienced. I think it really depends on if you want that person to take on a lot more and be almost part of your founding team. And do you want to find someone that is going to join your leadership team? (01:02:38): The other option I guess is you could also just bring on an advisor and that advisor is someone that's not full time. It can even guide if you hire someone that's a bit earlier, guide that person and that is a really good combination. And so it really depends on the context, who's also on the current team and who you want to bring into. Are you looking for an actual leader that's going to scale with the company or are you not ready quite yet for that?
turns.zh:
这实际上取决于团队当前的构成。创始人本身或现有团队对增长的重视程度有多高？如果他们对增长感兴趣，而更关注找人来执行任务，我认为可以考虑招聘职业生涯早期、具备强大第一性原理思维的人才。我认为这种选择存在成功与失败的风险——作为前咨询顾问，我过去常建议招募前顾问，但这种做法确实存在不确定性。还有一些价值所在，比如那些真正理解收购策略并有实际操作经验的人，他们或许能开拓出特定渠道。

（01:02:04）：所以我认为，要么选择有过收购经验的人（即使他们职业生涯早期），他们需要有强大的增长思维，但必须是第一性原理思考者；要么招募早期职业生涯的聪明人才，让他们参加Reforge课程，汲取知识；或者选择更有经验的人。我认为关键在于：你希望这个人承担更多职责，成为创始团队的一员，还是想招入领导团队？

（01:02:38）：另外，你也可以引入兼职顾问。这样既能指导早期员工，又能形成良好的协同效应。这完全取决于现有团队的构成，以及你希望引入的人才类型。你是在寻找能随公司一起成长的领导者，还是还没准备好迎接这样的挑战？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about in terms of their skillset? I imagine if you're kind of feeling like paid growth is going to be your main acquisition channel, you probably want to find someone that's really good at that versus it might be a virality, product led growth stuff, then you want to find maybe a product range of person. How much weight do you put into that skillset in that first hire?
turns.zh: 那技能方面呢？我猜如果你认为付费增长将成为主要的收购渠道，你可能需要找精通这方面的人；但如果是病毒式传播、产品主导的增长策略，那或许更适合产品经理背景的人才。在首轮招聘中，你会更看重哪方面的技能？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I actually think it's less about expertise in skillset, if that makes sense. And more there a ability to, again, I think of it like a portfolio manager. So this is more on the growth marketing side and bringing in acquisition. They are managing a portfolio and they're trying to figure out what works. I actually think you need to find someone that's analytical for this role, but that also understands things like who is the user? They're really creative in finding the user. And so it's actually looking for attributes but not expertise. (01:03:58): I actually think the more expertise someone has, the more it actually can lead to a false precision and then thinking they know what they're going to do. And especially, I don't think you actually need paid marketing expertise until much later when you're starting to think about incrementality or you're managing all these campaigns. I actually think the expertise is more important later. And then similarly on product growth, I actually think product growth is not higher till much later. A lot of early stage companies don't even have a product manager until later. And so I find that a growth product person isn't until much later down the road.
turns.zh:
实际上，我认为重点不在于专业技能（如果这能说得通的话），而在于能力——就像投资组合经理一样。他们需要管理增长营销组合，探索有效的策略。我认为这个角色更需要分析能力，同时要理解用户是谁。他们需要善于创新地找到用户。所以关键在于寻找特质而非专业知识。

（01:03:58）：我认为专业知识过多反而可能导致错误的精确感，让人误以为自己知道该怎么做。特别是，直到你开始考虑增量效应或管理多个广告活动时，才真正需要付费营销的专业知识。专业知识在后期阶段更为重要。同样，在产品增长方面，也要等到后期才有更高的要求。许多初创公司甚至要到后期才引入产品经理。所以我认为产品增长专家通常在后期才出现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a couple more questions. One is, you mentioned that it sometimes makes sense to bring on an advisor. I know sometimes companies have a bad time with advisors that just don't provide much value and they're giving equity. Other times it's transformative. Some of the stories you've shared, when is it appropriate to hire an advisor and is there any, I guess advice for what to look for in a growth advisor at this early stage, especially?
turns.zh: 还有几个问题。首先，你提到有时引入顾问是有意义的。我知道有些公司与顾问合作效果不佳，因为顾问提供不了太多价值却被授予股权；而有些合作则带来了变革性的影响。你分享的案例中，何时适合聘请顾问？尤其是在初期阶段，如何评估一位增长顾问的价值？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I would add an advisor if there is probably a knowledge gap on the team is I would say. And their advisors come in so many different forms too, and everyone does it slightly differently. For some folks, it's a monthly call for other times, especially when I'm full-time advising, I'll have weekly calls. I'll even join some team meetings. I'll look at mocks. And so everyone does it slightly differently. And so I think it depends on what you're looking for. I would definitely say that even getting to know the individual and making sure you're on the same page on what you're looking for and what the goals are. And then what I've done in the past too is initially set up a shorter engagement, like a quarter long engagement and then decide if you want to go longer. (01:05:47): And I also think it's fine to, let's say you have an advisor agreement, you're not getting value to basically part ways. If it's not, you're not finding value. I think every advisor wants to make sure they're adding value. So I definitely think to summarize, being really explicit on what advice you're looking for and making sure you're on the same page of what you want. And then also set up a try before you buy if you want to do a quarter long engagement first. And knowing you can always part ways if it's not a fit even before that period of time.
turns.zh: 我认为，如果团队存在知识缺口，就可以考虑引入顾问。顾问的形式多种多样，每个人的合作方式也各不相同。对有些人来说，每月一次通话即可；而对于我全职担任顾问的项目，则会每周通话，甚至参与团队会议和审阅模拟方案。关键在于明确合作目标，确保双方对期望达成共识。我建议先签订短期合作协议，比如一个季度试用期，到期后再决定是否延长合作。（01:05:47）如果合作未能创造价值，及时结束合作也很正常。毕竟顾问都希望能提供真正的价值。总结来说，关键在于清晰传达你的需求，保持一致的目标定位。若想试水合作，不妨先签订一个季度的试用协议。即使合作不顺利，也能在试用期内及时止损。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question before we get to a very exciting lightning round. You've brought up this concept of first principles thinking. I'm curious how you measure that and how you get a sense of, is this person strong at first principles thinking?
turns.zh: 在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节前，最后一个问题。你提到了第一性原理思维，我想了解如何评估一个人的第一性原理思维能力？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: It's definitely a word I use a lot. First principles thinking, I think of it as you are not using a set framework and set formula, but you're creating your own based on the context that you're getting. And so when I think about first principles thinking often it is knowing what questions to ask so that you can start forming a mental model. And then it is actually starting to form that mental model and then knowing to evolve it and knowing when it's not working and really coming from a place of curiosity of is this really working? This is something that I'm known for on my team as well, which is I ask tons of questions, but it doesn't come from a place of wanting to show that I'm asking good questions or anything that comes from a place of trying to solve the problem and making sure that we're always solving the problem at hand, making sure we're doing the right things. (01:07:28): If there's new information, do we actually still want to do it this way? And so I think first principles thinking is often about asking questions and then creating your own framework. That's how I would define it. And it's maybe another way to describe it is critical thinking. It's like you're able to think very critically, and I think it's important to, at least for me, create a culture where that's okay. I think the moment you have a culture where people aren't asking questions aren't constantly revisiting their work, that's when you're not maybe pushing yourself to do your best work. And I think it also just creates a fun environment where we're like, "Oh yeah, why are we doing this?" And really leading with your curiosity.
turns.zh:
这绝对是我常用的术语。所谓第一性原理思维，我认为它意味着你并非依赖既定的框架或公式，而是根据手头的情境构建自己的思考体系。因此，当我思考第一性原理思维时，通常会想到：首先要学会提问，以此搭建思维模型；然后着手构建这个思维模型，并在模型失效时及时调整。这种思维模式的核心在于保持好奇心——我问的问题多吗？但这绝不是为了炫耀，而是为了真正解决问题、确保我们始终专注于手头任务。

（01:07:28）：如果有新信息出现，我们是否还应该坚持原有做法？在我看来，第一性原理思维的核心在于提问并构建自己的框架。或许用批判性思维来描述它更为贴切。这种思维模式能让人进行深度思考，而对我来说，营造一个允许这种思维的文化氛围至关重要。一旦团队成员停止提问、不再反思工作成果时，创新动力就会减弱。我认为这种文化还能营造出有趣的氛围，比如大家会问：“哦，对了，我们为什么要这么做？”这种好奇心驱动的探索精神，正是推动我们创造最佳成果的动力源泉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of a person or moment or question that comes to mind of this is an epitome of a first principles thinker moment or question or a way of approaching something?
turns.zh: 你能否举个例子，说明某个人、某个时刻或某个问题体现了第一性原理思维的典范特质？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: My aha moment of the value of first principles thinking was when I was at Dropbox and we had the most unconventional people on our initial sales team. Dropbox was known for this. We would hire a ton of really smart people that had never done sales and had them do sales. There were a lot of disadvantages to that, I think. We were figuring a lot of things out. Maybe we should have split, had a few people that knew sales better and a combo of both. But I do think it led to a ton of innovation. Even I actually started on the sales team, this is a fun fact. I used to answer the 1-800 number at Dropbox, and if you go to Dropbox's website, you see a chat level. I used to also do that role, and so I think that what we got from that was that's how we got our very innovative go-to-market motions. (01:09:03): That also gave a ton of people, 'cause a lot of those people then moved into different functions at the company. They had all this context on who the user was. They had talked to so many different users at that point, and that's actually what helped me a lot when I moved into growth is I had all that context and I learned from that going back to first principles thinking that if you take people that are just super smart, they've never done it before, one advantage of that is they can innovate because I think they come in with, "I don't know anything. Let me just figure this out." Versus someone that think they know all the answers, limits you into what you are going to do. And so my aha moment was really at Dropbox seeing so many times people that had never done these things and then seeing so much innovation come as a result of that.
turns.zh:
我对第一性原理思维价值的顿悟时刻，发生在我在Dropbox工作的时候。当时我们初期销售团队成员非常不寻常，这也是Dropbox闻名于世的原因。我们会招聘大量从未做过销售但非常聪明的人来做销售工作。这其中存在诸多弊端，我认为我们当时正在摸索很多东西。或许我们本该分开团队，既有更懂销售的人，也有兼具销售和其他技能的人。但我认为这确实催生了大量创新。说个趣事，我最初也是销售团队的一员。我曾在Dropbox的1-800客服热线接听电话，如果你访问Dropbox官网，会看到一个聊天界面，我当时也负责这个角色。我认为正是通过这样的经历，我们才形成了极具创新性的市场推广策略。

（01:09:03）：这也让很多人受益，因为许多成员后来转到了公司的其他部门。他们对用户有了全面的了解，积累了与大量用户沟通的经验。这段经历对我后来转入增长团队也非常有帮助——我拥有这些背景知识，再回归到第一性原理思维，发现当你让那些从零开始的人加入团队时，他们能带来创新思维，因为他们会带着“我什么都不懂，先摸索”的心态。而那些自以为无所不知的人，反而会限制自己的行动空间。所以我在Dropbox的这段经历让我深刻认识到，允许那些从零开始的人加入团队，能激发创新火花。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an awesome story. Is there anything else you wanted to share or touch on before we get to or very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 这真是个精彩的故事。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享或探讨的吗？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I think that's it. I wanted to make sure, I know I talked a lot about developing people, so thank all the people that have helped develop me in my career and then especially thank all the folks that I've worked with and my team, especially the team at Webflow and particularly wanted to make sure to thank [Xing Lin 01:10:14], Rory Davidson and [Jo Wang01:10:16] who joined me from previous companies to Webflow.
turns.zh: 我想就这些了。我特别想感谢那些在职业生涯中帮助过我的人，也要特别感谢Webflow团队的每一位成员，尤其是[Xing Lin 01:10:14]、Rory Davidson和[Jo Wang01:10:16]，他们从之前的公司加入了Webflow。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shoutouts. Well, with that, Melissa, we have reached our very exciting lightning ground. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 致敬环节。好的，Melissa，我们现在要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我有六个问题要问你，你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: The first one is Leaders Eat Last. I really like that leadership book by Simon Sinek. Also two non-career related books is The Untethered Soul. It really has taught me a lot about being present and then also the Four Agreements, which is a very short and easy read, but good principles to live by.
turns.zh: 第一本是《领导者最后行动》。西蒙·斯涅克的这本领导力著作我很喜欢。另外两本与职业无关的书是《不羁的灵魂》，它让我深刻理解了活在当下，还有《四项约定》。这本书简短易读，但其中蕴含着值得遵循的生活准则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: This one isn't super recent, but Winning Time on HBO. It's about the LA Lakers during the '80s and the Showtime era. I'm originally from LA and grew up a Lakers fan, so it's a fun watch for me and a nice escape.
turns.zh: 这部不是很新的，但HBO的《winning time》不错。它讲述了80年代湖人队“Showtime”时代的故事。我来自洛杉矶，从小就是湖人队球迷，所以看这部剧很有趣，也能放松一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You'll love a new movie I just watched last night called Air, which is about how Nike got Michael Jordan signed. And it's similar vibes to that show.
turns.zh: 你会喜欢我昨晚刚看的一部新电影《Air》，讲的是耐克签下迈克尔·乔丹的故事。它和那部剧有相似的氛围。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yes, yes. I actually just watched that recently too.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。我最近也刚看过那部片子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Great.
turns.zh: 好的。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: That's a good one too. Yeah, I've watched all those basketball.
turns.zh: 那部片子也很不错。是的，我把那些篮球比赛都看完了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. I also grew up in LA. Also a huge Laker fan from-
turns.zh: 天哪。我也是在洛杉矶长大的。而且我一直是湖人队的超级粉丝，从——

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Oh, nice.
turns.zh: 哦，不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: From before. Next question, what's a favorite interview question you like to ask?
turns.zh: 很久以前的事了。下一个问题，你最喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: For me, it's not a question, but it's that stage of preparing before the presentation and getting a sense for what it's like to work with each other. I think that has been one of the best ways for me to get signal.
turns.zh: 对我来说，这不是个问题，但在准备演示前的那个阶段，了解彼此的合作方式，这对我来说一直是最好的获取信息的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you say more on that?
turns.zh: 你能再详细说说吗？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yes. So it's essentially that prep call before I ask them to do a presentation and going through the presentation together and working together on refining it.
turns.zh: 是的。所以基本上就是在让我做演示之前的那次准备通话，一起过一遍演示内容，共同打磨它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We already talked about that, so we'll move on. What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们已经讨论过这个了，所以我们继续下一个问题。你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: I feel like everyone's saying this, but ChatGPT. I feel like it has really changed everything. There's so many interesting ways to use it. My team at Webflow right now is also starting to think about incorporating AI into the product, and so yeah, I just think that is ... Yeah, so many things you can do with it.
turns.zh: 我感觉每个人都在说这个，但ChatGPT。我觉得它真的改变了一切。有很多有趣的使用方式。我在Webflow的团队现在也开始考虑把AI融入产品，所以是的，我觉得这……你能用它做太多事情了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is something relatively minor that you've changed in your product development process that has had a big impact on the way that your team executes?
turns.zh: 在产品开发过程中，你改变了什么相对较小的部分，却对团队的执行方式产生了重大影响？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: This one here is what I also spoke about for earlier, which is, I mean, thinking through your DACI. It sounds so simple, but I do think a lot of times teams are thinking through how do they work with other teams? Who is driving? Who is the decision maker? And so having a DACI, I have found is really helpful.
turns.zh: 前面我也提到过这个，就是，嗯，思考你的DACI。这听起来很简单，但我确实觉得很多团队都在思考如何与其他团队合作？谁在主导？谁是决策者？所以制定DACI，我发现真的很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, you've been at Webflow for a number of years. What is a favorite pro tip for using Webflow?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，你在Webflow工作了好几年了。对于使用Webflow，有什么最喜欢的专业建议吗？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah, I actually have two if that's okay.
turns.zh: 是的，如果可以的话，我有两个建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's good. Even better [inaudible 01:13:01].
turns.zh: 太好了。甚至更好了[1:13:01未录音]。

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So one is thing that I've often heard from folks is it's hard to learn Webflow. And so basically watching our university videos, which is where we teach Webflow while also building the designer, and we actually now enable to have the videos in the product, so you can do them side by side. And then the other one is our Figma to Webflow plugin, which is you can take a Figma design and then convert it to Webflow, which is a great hack if you already have a design in Figma.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。一个是我经常听到人们说Webflow很难学。所以基本上看我们的大学视频教程，就是我们一边教Webflow一边开发设计器，现在我们已经把视频集成到产品里了，所以你可以边看边操作。另一个是我们的Figma到Webflow插件，你可以把Figma设计转换成Webflow，如果你已经有Figma设计的话，这是一个很棒的技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I did not know that existed. That is a really smart idea and feature. Melissa, I could see why people follow you from company to company. I feel like the companies that are going to get to work with you in this new stage of your life are also very lucky. Thank you for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 哇，我不知道有这个功能。这真是个聪明的想法和功能。梅利莎，我能理解为什么人们会跟着你从一家公司跳到另一家公司。我觉得在你人生新阶段即将合作的公司也会很幸运。感谢你今天的到来。最后两个问题。读者如果想联系你，可以在哪里找到你？听众如何能对你有所帮助？

turns.speaker: Melissa Tan
turns.en: Folks can find me on LinkedIn, also on Twitter, Melissamtan, and then how can listeners be helpful to me? I mean, I love jamming on things, growth, thinking about leadership and managing, so if any of this resonates, reach out. I'd love to have a discussion and yeah.
turns.zh: 大家可以在领英上找到我，也可以在推特上关注我，账号是Melissamtan。那么，听众们如何能给我提供帮助呢？我的意思是，我热爱探讨成长、领导力和管理等话题，如果这些内容能引起你们共鸣，不妨联系我。我很乐意与大家展开深入交流，期待与你畅谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
